label: Definition 5.1.1
Example 5.1.2
proof:
\begin{proof}
We verify periodicity using Definition~5.1.1.

\textbf{(1) $2\pi$-periodicity of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.} For all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the standard trigonometric identities give
\[
\sin(x+2\pi)=\sin x,\qquad \cos(x+2\pi)=\cos x.
\]
Hence $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are $2\pi$-periodic.

\textbf{(2) $2\pi$-periodicity of $e^{ix}$.} For all $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
 e^{i(x+2\pi)}=e^{ix}e^{i2\pi}=e^{ix},
\]
since $e^{i2\pi}=1$. Thus $e^{ix}$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

\textbf{(3) Periods $4\pi,6\pi,\dots$.} If $f$ is $2\pi$-periodic, then for any integer $k$,
\[
 f(x+2\pi k)=f(x)
\]
by repeated application of $f(x+2\pi)=f(x)$ (and for negative $k$ by applying the identity to $x-2\pi$). Hence $4\pi,6\pi,\dots$ are also periods.

\textbf{(4) Non-periodicity of $f(x)=x$.} Suppose there exists $L>0$ such that $x+L=x$ for all $x$. Then $L=0$, contradicting $L>0$. Hence $f(x)=x$ is not periodic.

\textbf{(5) Constant function.} If $f(x)\equiv 1$, then for any $L>0$ and all $x$,
\[
 f(x+L)=1=f(x),
\]
so $f$ is $L$-periodic for every $L>0$.
\end{proof}

label: Corollary 5.1.1
content:
\begin{corollary}[$kL$-shift invariance]
If a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is $L$-periodic, then
\[
f(x+kL)=f(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and all }k\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]
In particular, if $f$ is $1$-periodic, then $f(x+k)=f(x)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{corollary}
proof: From $f(x+L)=f(x)$, use induction for $k\ge 0$; for $k<0$, apply the $k>0$ case to $x+kL$ (or substitute $x\mapsto x-kL$) to obtain the negative shifts. The case $k=0$ is trivial.

label: Definition 5.1.2
content:
\begin{definition}[$\mathbb{Z}$-periodic and $L\mathbb{Z}$-periodic]
A function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is called \emph{$\mathbb{Z}$-periodic} if it is $1$-periodic, i.e.
\[
f(x+1)=f(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
More generally, for $L>0$, an $L$-periodic function is sometimes also called \emph{$L\mathbb{Z}$-periodic}.
\end{definition}

label: Example 5.1.4
proof:
\begin{proof}
We use the definition of $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic (equivalently, $1$-periodic): $f(x+1)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

\textbf{(1) Trigonometric/exponential examples.}
Let $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. For all $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\cos\bigl(2\pi n(x+1)\bigr)=\cos(2\pi n x+2\pi n)=\cos(2\pi n x),
\]
\[
\sin\bigl(2\pi n(x+1)\bigr)=\sin(2\pi n x+2\pi n)=\sin(2\pi n x),
\]
using that adding an integer multiple of $2\pi$ does not change $\sin$ or $\cos$. Also,
\[
 e^{2\pi i n(x+1)}=e^{2\pi i n x}\,e^{2\pi i n}=e^{2\pi i n x},
\]
since $e^{2\pi i n}=1$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Hence all three functions are $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic.

\textbf{What if $n\notin\mathbb{Z}$?}
If $n\notin\mathbb{Z}$, then $e^{2\pi i n(x+1)}=e^{2\pi i n x}e^{2\pi i n}\neq e^{2\pi i n x}$, because $e^{2\pi i n}\neq 1$. Thus $e^{2\pi i n x}$ is not $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic. Likewise, $\cos(2\pi n x)$ and $\sin(2\pi n x)$ are $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic if and only if $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.

\textbf{(2) Square wave.}
Define $f$ by
\[
 f(x)=1 \text{ if } x\in\bigl[k,k+\tfrac12\bigr),\qquad f(x)=0 \text{ if } x\in\bigl[k+\tfrac12,k+1\bigr)
\]
for the unique integer $k$ with $x\in[k,k+1)$.
Then for any $x\in\mathbb{R}$, if $x\in[k,k+1)$, we have $x+1\in[k+1,k+2)$ and the membership of $x$ in the first half $[k,k+\tfrac12)$ or second half $[k+\tfrac12,k+1)$ is preserved after shifting by $1$. Hence $f(x+1)=f(x)$ for all $x$, so $f$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 5.1.3
content:
\begin{definition}[Integer part and fractional part]
For any real number $x\in\mathbb{R}$, we define the \emph{integer part} of $x$, denoted $[x]$,
to be the unique integer $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
\[
k \le x < k+1.
\]
We then define the \emph{fractional part} of $x$, denoted $\{x\}$, by
\[
\{x\} := x - [x].
\]
\end{definition}

label: Lemma 5.1.5a
proof:
\begin{proof}
Since $f$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic, we have
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |f(x)| = \sup_{x\in[0,1]} |f(x)|.
\]
Indeed, for any $x\in\mathbb{R}$ we can write $x=k+y$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $y\in[0,1)$, and then
$|f(x)| = |f(y)|$ by periodicity.

Now $f$ is continuous on the compact interval $[0,1]$, hence $|f|$ is continuous on $[0,1]$.
By the extreme value theorem, $|f|$ attains a maximum on $[0,1]$; i.e. there exists $M>0$ such that
$|f(x)|\le M$ for all $x\in[0,1]$. By the reduction above, this holds for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.1.5b
proof:
\begin{proof}
\emph{Periodicity:} For any $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
(f\pm g)(x+1)=f(x+1)\pm g(x+1)=f(x)\pm g(x)=(f\pm g)(x),
\]
\[
(fg)(x+1)=f(x+1)g(x+1)=f(x)g(x)=(fg)(x),
\]
and for $c\in\mathbb{C}$,
\[
(cf)(x+1)=c f(x+1)=c f(x)=(cf)(x).
\]
So these functions are $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic.

\emph{Continuity:} Sums, differences, and products of continuous functions are continuous, and scalar multiples
of continuous functions are continuous. Hence $f\pm g$, $fg$, and $cf$ are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.
Therefore they all lie in $C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.1.5c
proof:
\begin{proof}
Assume $(f_n)$ is a sequence in $C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$.

\emph{Periodicity of the limit:} Fix $x\in\mathbb{R}$. For every $n$, $f_n(x+1)=f_n(x)$.
Taking $n\to\infty$ gives
\[
f(x+1)=\lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x+1)=\lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)=f(x),
\]
so $f$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic.

\emph{Continuity of the limit:} Fix $x_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$.
Choose $N$ such that $\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |f_N(x)-f(x)| < \varepsilon/3$.
Since $f_N$ is continuous at $x_0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that
$|x-x_0|<\delta$ implies $|f_N(x)-f_N(x_0)|<\varepsilon/3$.
Then for $|x-x_0|<\delta$,
\[
|f(x)-f(x_0)|
\le |f(x)-f_N(x)| + |f_N(x)-f_N(x_0)| + |f_N(x_0)-f(x_0)|
< \varepsilon.
\]
Thus $f$ is continuous at $x_0$, and hence continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.
Therefore $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 5.2.1
content:
\begin{definition}[Inner product]
If $f,g\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$, we define
\[
\langle f,g\rangle := \int_{[0,1]} f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx.
\]
\end{definition}

label: Example 5.2.3
proof:
\begin{proof}
By definition of the inner product,
\[
\langle f,g\rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx = \int_{0}^{1} 1\cdot e^{-2\pi i x}\,dx.
\]
Compute:
\[
\int_{0}^{1} e^{-2\pi i x}\,dx
= \left.\frac{e^{-2\pi i x}}{-2\pi i}\right|_{0}^{1}
= \frac{e^{-2\pi i}-1}{-2\pi i}
=0,
\]
since $e^{-2\pi i}=1$. Hence $\langle f,g\rangle=0$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.5a
proof:
\begin{proof}
We compute
\[
\langle g,f\rangle=\int_{0}^{1} g(x)\overline{f(x)}\,dx.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\overline{\langle f,g\rangle}
=\overline{\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx}
=\int_{0}^{1} \overline{f(x)\overline{g(x)}}\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1} \overline{f(x)}\,g(x)\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1} g(x)\overline{f(x)}\,dx
=\langle g,f\rangle.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.5b
proof:
\begin{proof}
We have
\[
\langle f,f\rangle=\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{f(x)}\,dx=\int_{0}^{1} |f(x)|^2\,dx\ge 0.
\]
If $f\equiv 0$, then clearly $\langle f,f\rangle=0$.
Conversely, assume $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, i.e.
\[
\int_{0}^{1}|f(x)|^2\,dx=0.
\]
If $f$ is not identically zero, then there exists $x_0\in[0,1]$ such that $f(x_0)\neq 0$,
hence $|f(x_0)|^2>0$. Since $f$ is continuous, $|f|^2$ is continuous, so there exist
$\delta>0$ and $c>0$ such that $|f(x)|^2\ge c$ whenever $|x-x_0|<\delta$.
Therefore
\[
\int_{0}^{1}|f(x)|^2\,dx
\ge \int_{(x_0-\delta,\,x_0+\delta)\cap[0,1]} c\,dx
>0,
\]
a contradiction. Thus $f\equiv 0$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.5c
content:
\begin{lemma}[Properties of the inner product (c)]
(Linearity in the first variable) For $f,g,h\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and $c\in\mathbb{C}$,
$\langle f+g,h\rangle=\langle f,h\rangle+\langle g,h\rangle$ and $\langle cf,g\rangle=c\langle f,g\rangle$.
\end{lemma}
proof:
\begin{proof}
By linearity of the integral,
\[
\langle f+g,h\rangle
=\int_{0}^{1}(f(x)+g(x))\overline{h(x)}\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1}f(x)\overline{h(x)}\,dx+\int_{0}^{1}g(x)\overline{h(x)}\,dx
=\langle f,h\rangle+\langle g,h\rangle.
\]
Also, for $c\in\mathbb{C}$,
\[
\langle cf,g\rangle
=\int_{0}^{1}(cf(x))\overline{g(x)}\,dx
=c\int_{0}^{1}f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx
=c\langle f,g\rangle.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.5d
content:
\begin{lemma}[Properties of the inner product (d)]
(Antilinearity in the second variable) For $f,g,h\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and $c\in\mathbb{C}$,
$\langle f,g+h\rangle=\langle f,g\rangle+\langle f,h\rangle$ and $\langle f,cg\rangle=\overline{c}\,\langle f,g\rangle$.
\end{lemma}
proof:
\begin{proof}
First,
\[
\langle f,g+h\rangle
=\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{g(x)+h(x)}\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\big(\overline{g(x)}+\overline{h(x)}\big)\,dx
=\langle f,g\rangle+\langle f,h\rangle.
\]
Next,
\[
\langle f,cg\rangle
=\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{c\,g(x)}\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\,\overline{c}\,\overline{g(x)}\,dx
=\overline{c}\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx
=\overline{c}\,\langle f,g\rangle.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Example 5.2.6
proof:
\begin{proof}
By definition of the $L^2$ norm,
\[
\|f\|_2 = \left(\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{f(x)}\,dx\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Since $\overline{e^{2\pi i x}}=e^{-2\pi i x}$, we have $f(x)\overline{f(x)}=e^{2\pi i x}e^{-2\pi i x}=1$. Hence
\[
\|f\|_2 = \left(\int_{0}^{1} 1\,dx\right)^{1/2} = 1.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Exercise 5.2.3
content:
\begin{exercise}
If $f \in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}; \mathbb{C})$ is non-zero, show that $0 < \|f\|_2 \leq \|f\|_{L^{\infty}}$. Conversely, if $0 < A \leq B$ are real numbers, show that there exists a non-zero function $f \in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}; \mathbb{C})$ such that $\|f\|_2 = A$ and $\|f\|_{L^{\infty}} = B$. (Hint: let $g$ be a non-constant non-negative real-valued function in $C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}; \mathbb{C})$, and consider functions $f = (c + dg)^{1/2}$ for some constant real numbers $c,d > 0$.)\end{exercise}
proof:
\begin{proof}
(1) If $f\neq 0$, then $|f|^2$ is continuous and not identically $0$, hence $\int_0^1 |f(x)|^2\,dx>0$, so $\|f\|_2>0$.
Also, for all $x$, $|f(x)|\le \|f\|_{L^\infty}$, hence
\[
\|f\|_2^2=\int_0^1 |f(x)|^2\,dx\le \int_0^1 \|f\|_{L^\infty}^2\,dx=\|f\|_{L^\infty}^2,
\]
so $\|f\|_2\le \|f\|_{L^\infty}$.

(2) Conversely, fix $0<A\le B$. Choose a non-constant non-negative $g\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{R})$ with $\|g\|_{L^\infty}=1$.
Let $f=(c+d g)^{1/2}$ with $c,d>0$. Then $\|f\|_{L^\infty}=\sqrt{c+d}$.
Pick $c+d=B^2$ so that $\|f\|_{L^\infty}=B$.
Also
\[
\|f\|_2^2=\int_0^1 (c+d g(x))\,dx=c+d\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx.
\]
Since $g$ is not constant and $0\le g\le 1$, we have $0<\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx<1$.
With $c=B^2-d$, the quantity $\|f\|_2^2$ varies continuously from $B^2\int_0^1 g$ (when $d\to B^2$) to $B^2$ (when $d\to 0$), hence attains every value in $(B^2\int_0^1 g,\,B^2)$.
Choose $d$ so that $\|f\|_2^2=A^2$; then $\|f\|_2=A$ and $\|f\|_{L^\infty}=B$, with $f\neq 0$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.7a
Lemma 5.2.7b
proof:
\begin{proof}
If $\|g\|_2=0$, then $g=0$ by Lemma~5.2.7a and the inequality is trivial.
Assume $\|g\|_2>0$. For any $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, positivity gives
\[
0\le \langle f-\lambda g, f-\lambda g\rangle.
\]
Expand using Lemma~5.2.5c--d and Hermitian symmetry:
\[
\langle f-\lambda g, f-\lambda g\rangle
=\|f\|_2^2 -2\Re\big(\overline{\lambda}\langle f,g\rangle\big)+|\lambda|^2\|g\|_2^2.
\]
Choose $\lambda=\langle f,g\rangle/\|g\|_2^2$ to obtain
\[
0\le \|f\|_2^2-\frac{|\langle f,g\rangle|^2}{\|g\|_2^2},
\]
hence $|\langle f,g\rangle|^2\le \|f\|_2^2\|g\|_2^2$, and taking square roots gives the result.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.7c
proof:
\begin{proof}
Compute
\[
\|f+g\|_2^2=\langle f+g,f+g\rangle=\|f\|_2^2+2\Re\langle f,g\rangle+\|g\|_2^2
\le \|f\|_2^2+2|\langle f,g\rangle|+\|g\|_2^2.
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz (Lemma~5.2.7b), $|\langle f,g\rangle|\le \|f\|_2\|g\|_2$, so
\[
\|f+g\|_2^2\le (\|f\|_2+\|g\|_2)^2.
\]
Taking square roots yields $\|f+g\|_2\le \|f\|_2+\|g\|_2$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.7d
proof:
\begin{proof}
If $\langle f,g\rangle=0$, then $\langle g,f\rangle=\overline{\langle f,g\rangle}=0$ by Lemma~5.2.5a.
Therefore
\[
\|f+g\|_2^2=\langle f+g,f+g\rangle=\langle f,f\rangle+\langle f,g\rangle+\langle g,f\rangle+\langle g,g\rangle=\|f\|_2^2+\|g\|_2^2.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.2.7e
proof:
\begin{proof}
We compute
\[
\|cf\|_2^2=\langle cf,cf\rangle=\int_0^1 (cf(x))\overline{(cf(x))}\,dx=\int_0^1 |c|^2|f(x)|^2\,dx=|c|^2\|f\|_2^2.
\]
Taking square roots gives $\|cf\|_2=|c|\,\|f\|_2$.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 5.2.2
Definition 5.2.3
content:
\begin{definition}[$L^2$-convergence]\label{def:5.2.Y}
Let $(f_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence in $C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and let $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$. We say that $f_n$ \emph{converges to $f$ in the $L^2$ metric} (or \emph{in $L^2$}) if
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{L^2}(f_n,f)=0,
\]
that is, equivalently,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} \int_{0}^{1} |f_n(x)-f(x)|^2\,dx = 0.
\]
\end{definition}

label: Definition 5.3.1
content:
\begin{definition}[Characters]
For every integer $n$, define $e_n\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ by
\[
e_n(x):=e^{2\pi i n x}.
\]
\end{definition}

label: Definition 5.3.2
content:
\begin{definition}[Trigonometric polynomials]
A function $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ is a trigonometric polynomial if
\[
f=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n e_n
\]
for some integer $N\ge 0$ and complex numbers $(c_n)_{n=-N}^N$.
\end{definition}

label: Lemma 5.3.5
content:
\begin{lemma}[Characters are an orthonormal system]
For any integers $n,m$,
\[
\langle e_n,e_m\rangle = \begin{cases}1,& n=m\\ 0,& n\ne m\end{cases}
\]
and $\|e_n\|_2=1$.
\end{lemma}
proof:
\begin{proof}
Recall that $e_n(x)=e^{2\pi i n x}$ and
\[
\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx.
\]
Fix integers $n,m$. Then
\[
\langle e_n,e_m\rangle
=\int_{0}^{1} e^{2\pi i n x}\,\overline{e^{2\pi i m x}}\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1} e^{2\pi i (n-m)x}\,dx.
\]
If $n=m$, then the integrand is identically $1$, so $\langle e_n,e_n\rangle=1$.
If $n\neq m$, set $k:=n-m\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$; then
\[
\int_{0}^{1} e^{2\pi i k x}\,dx
=\left[\frac{e^{2\pi i k x}}{2\pi i k}\right]_{0}^{1}
=\frac{e^{2\pi i k}-1}{2\pi i k}=0.
\]
Hence $\langle e_n,e_m\rangle$ equals $1$ if $n=m$ and $0$ otherwise, and therefore
$\|e_n\|_2=\sqrt{\langle e_n,e_n\rangle}=1$.
\end{proof}

label: Corollary 5.3.6
content:
\begin{corollary}
Let $f=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n e_n$ be a trigonometric polynomial. Then
\[
c_n=\langle f,e_n\rangle\quad (-N\le n\le N),
\]
and $\langle f,e_n\rangle=0$ if $n>N$ or $n<-N$. Also,
\[
\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} |c_n|^2.
\]
\end{corollary}
proof:
\begin{proof}
Fix $m\in\mathbb{Z}$. By linearity,
\[
\langle f,e_m\rangle=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n\langle e_n,e_m\rangle.
\]
By Lemma~5.3.5, this equals $c_m$ if $|m|\le N$ and $0$ otherwise.
For the norm,
\[
\|f\|_2^2=\langle f,f\rangle=\sum_{n=-N}^{N}\sum_{m=-N}^{N} c_n\overline{c_m}\langle e_n,e_m\rangle
=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} |c_n|^2.
\]
\end{proof}

label: Definition 5.3.7
content:
\begin{definition}[Fourier transform]
For $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, define the $n$-th Fourier coefficient
\[
\hat f(n):=\langle f,e_n\rangle = \int_{[0,1]} f(x)e^{-2\pi i n x}\,dx.
\]
The function $\hat f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ is called the Fourier transform of $f$.
\end{definition}

label: Definition 5.3.8
content:
\begin{definition}[Fourier inversion, Fourier series, and Plancherel formula]
\label{def:5.3.8}
Let $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and let $\hat f(n)$ denote its Fourier coefficients (as in Definition~5.3.7).

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Fourier series of $f$.} The formal series
\[
\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \hat f(n) e_n\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \hat f(n) e^{2\pi i n x}
\]
is called the \emph{Fourier series} of $f$.

\item \textbf{Fourier inversion formula (finite/trigonometric-polynomial case).} If $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial, then
\[
 f = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \hat f(n) e_n
\]
(where only finitely many terms are nonzero).

\item \textbf{Plancherel (Parseval) formula (finite/trigonometric-polynomial case).} If $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial, then
\[
\|f\|_2^2 = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} |\hat f(n)|^2.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

label: Theorem 5.4.1
content:
\begin{theorem}[Weierstrass approximation theorem for trigonometric polynomials]
Let $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. Then there exists a trigonometric polynomial $P$ such that
\[
\|f-P\|_\infty\le \varepsilon.
\]
\end{theorem}
proof:
\begin{proof}
Let $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$. By Lemma~5.1.5a, there exists $M>0$ such that $|f(x)|\le M$ for all $x$.
Let $\varepsilon>0$. By uniform continuity, choose $0<\delta<1/2$ so that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le\varepsilon$ whenever $|x-y|\le\delta$.
By Lemma~5.4.6, choose a trigonometric polynomial $P$ that is a periodic $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ approximation to the identity.
Then $f*P$ is a trigonometric polynomial. For any $x$,
\[
|f(x)-(f*P)(x)|\le \int_0^1 P(y)|f(x)-f(x-y)|\,dy.
\]
Split $[0,1]=[0,\delta]\cup[\delta,1-\delta]\cup[1-\delta,1]$ and use (i) uniform continuity on the first and last pieces, (ii) $|f|\le M$ and $P\le\varepsilon$ on the middle piece, to obtain
\[
|f(x)-(f*P)(x)|\le (2M+1)\varepsilon.
\]
Taking the supremum over $x$ yields $\|f-f*P\|_\infty\le (2M+1)\varepsilon$, and choosing $\varepsilon$ suitably gives the desired approximation.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 5.4.2
content:
\begin{definition}[Periodic convolution]
Let $f,g\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$. Define
\[
(f*g)(x):=\int_{[0,1]} f(y)g(x-y)\,dy.
\]
\end{definition}

label: Lemma 5.4.4a
proof:
\begin{proof}
We show $f*g$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic and continuous.

\emph{Periodicity:} for any $x$,
\[
(f*g)(x+1)=\int_0^1 f(y)g(x+1-y)\,dy=\int_0^1 f(y)g(x-y)\,dy=(f*g)(x),
\]
since $g$ is $1$-periodic.

\emph{Continuity:} $f$ is bounded on $[0,1]$; let $M=\sup_{y\in[0,1]}|f(y)|$.
Since $g$ is uniformly continuous, for $x'\to x$ we have $\sup_{y\in[0,1]}|g(x'-y)-g(x-y)|\to 0$.
Thus
\[
|(f*g)(x')-(f*g)(x)|\le \int_0^1 |f(y)|\,|g(x'-y)-g(x-y)|\,dy\le M\sup_{y\in[0,1]}|g(x'-y)-g(x-y)|\to 0.
\]
Hence $f*g$ is continuous and $\mathbb{Z}$-periodic.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.4.4b
proof:
\begin{proof}
For any $x$,
\[
(f*g)(x)=\int_0^1 f(y)g(x-y)\,dy.
\]
Substitute $t=x-y$ to get
\[
(f*g)(x)=\int_{x-1}^{x} f(x-t)g(t)\,dt.
\]
Using $1$-periodicity of $f$ and $g$, the integral over any length-$1$ interval equals the integral over $[0,1]$:
\[
\int_{x-1}^{x} f(x-t)g(t)\,dt=\int_0^1 f(x-t)g(t)\,dt=(g*f)(x).
\]
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.4.4c
proof:
\begin{proof}
All identities follow from linearity of the integral. For example,
\[
(f*(g+h))(x)=\int_0^1 f(y)(g+h)(x-y)\,dy=(f*g)(x)+(f*h)(x).
\]
Similarly
\[
((f+g)*h)(x)=\int_0^1 (f+g)(y)h(x-y)\,dy=(f*h)(x)+(g*h)(x),
\]
and for $c\in\mathbb{C}$,
\[
(c(f*g))(x)=c\int_0^1 f(y)g(x-y)\,dy=\int_0^1 (cf)(y)g(x-y)\,dy=((cf)*g)(x),
\]
and likewise $c(f*g)=f*(cg)$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 5.4.5
content:
Let $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
 f*e_n = \hat f(n)\,e_n.
\]
More generally, if $P=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n e_n$ is a trigonometric polynomial, then
\[
 f*P = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat f(n)c_n\,e_n,
\]
and in particular $f*P$ is a trigonometric polynomial.
proof:
For $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
(f*e_n)(x)=\int_{0}^{1} f(y)\,e_n(x-y)\,dy
=\int_{0}^{1} f(y)e^{2\pi i n(x-y)}\,dy
=e^{2\pi i n x}\int_{0}^{1} f(y)e^{-2\pi i n y}\,dy
=\hat f(n)e^{2\pi i n x}
=\hat f(n)e_n(x).
\]
If $P=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n e_n$, then by bilinearity of convolution,
\[
 f*P = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n(f*e_n)=\sum_{n=-N}^{N} c_n\hat f(n)e_n.
\]
Hence $f*P$ is a trigonometric polynomial.

label: Definition 5.4.5
content:
\begin{definition}[Periodic approximation to the identity]
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $0<\delta<1/2$. A function $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$ is a periodic $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ approximation to the identity if:

(a) $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$ and $\int_{[0,1]} f = 1$.

(b) $f(x)<\varepsilon$ for all $\delta\le |x|\le 1-\delta$.
\end{definition}

label: Lemma 5.4.6
Theorem 5.5.1
content:
\begin{theorem}[Fourier theorem]
For any $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$, the series $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \hat f(n)e_n$ converges to $f$ in $L^2$ metric:
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\left\|f-\sum_{n=-N}^{N}\hat f(n)e_n\right\|_2=0.
\]
\end{theorem}
proof:
Proof Let \( \varepsilon > 0 \). We have to show that there exists an \( N_0 \) such that \( \|f - \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n)e_n\|_2 \leq \varepsilon \) for all sufficiently large \( N \).

By the Weierstrass approximation theorem (Theorem 5.4.1), we can find a trigonometric polynomial \( P = \sum_{n=-N_0}^{N_0} c_n e_n \) such that \( \|f - P\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon \), for some \( N_0 > 0 \). In particular we have \( \|f - P\|_2 \leq \varepsilon \).

Now let \( N > N_0 \), and let \( F_N := \sum_{n=-N}^{n=N} \hat{f}(n)e_n \). We claim that \( \|f - F_N\|_2 \leq \varepsilon \). First observe that for any \( |m| \leq N \), we have

\[
\langle f - F_N, e_m \rangle = \langle f, e_m \rangle - \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n) \langle e_n, e_m \rangle = \hat{f}(m) - \hat{f}(m) = 0,
\]

where we have used Lemma 5.3.5. In particular we have

\[
\langle f - F_N, F_N - P \rangle = 0
\]

since we can write \( F_N - P \) as a linear combination of the \( e_m \) for which \( |m| \leq N \). By Pythagoras’ theorem we therefore have

\[
\|f - P\|_2^2 = \|f - F_N\|_2^2 + \|F_N - P\|_2^2
\]

and in particular

\[
\|f - F_N\|_2 \leq \|f - P\|_2 \leq \varepsilon.
\]

label: Theorem 5.5.3
proof:
Proof By the Weierstrass \(M\)-test (Theorem 3.5.7), we see that \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(n)e_n\) converges to some function \(F\), which by Lemma~5.1.5c is also continuous and \(\mathbb{Z}\)-periodic. Thus

\[\lim_{N \to \infty} \left\| F - \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n)e_n \right\|_{\infty} = 0\]

which implies that

\[\lim_{N \to \infty} \left\| F - \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n)e_n \right\|_{2} = 0\]

since $\|\cdot\|_2\le \|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ (using boundedness from Lemma~5.1.5a). But the same partial sums converge in $L^2$ to $f$ by the Fourier theorem, hence $F=f$, and the uniform convergence follows.

label: Theorem 5.5.4
content:
\begin{theorem}[Plancherel / Parseval]
For any $f\in C(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$, the series $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} |\hat f(n)|^2$ converges and
\[
\|f\|_2^2 = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |\hat f(n)|^2.
\]
\end{theorem}
proof:
Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). By the Fourier theorem we know that

\[ \left\| f - \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n)e_n \right\|_2 \leq \varepsilon \]

if \(N\) is large enough. In particular,

\[ \| f \|_2 - \varepsilon \leq \left\| \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n)e_n \right\|_2 \leq \| f \|_2 + \varepsilon. \]

By Corollary 5.3.6,

\[ \left\| \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \hat{f}(n)e_n \right\|_2^2 = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} |\hat{f}(n)|^2. \]

Hence

\[ (\| f \|_2 - \varepsilon)^2 \leq \sum_{n=-N}^{N} |\hat{f}(n)|^2 \leq (\| f \|_2 + \varepsilon)^2. \]

Letting $N\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\to 0$ yields
\[\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |\hat f(n)|^2 = \|f\|_2^2.\]
